**Claim.** Yes. Every prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_K$ lying above $p$ (i.e. with $\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=p\mathbb{Z}$) appears among the factors $\mathfrak{P}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{P}_n$ in the prime decomposition $p\mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{P}_1\cdots\mathfrak{P}_n$.

**Proof.**

Let $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_K$ be a nonzero prime ideal lying above $p$, so $\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=p\mathbb{Z}$.

**Step 1: $p\mathcal{O}_K\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$.**
Since $p\in p\mathbb{Z}=\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$, the element $p$ belongs to $\mathfrak{P}$. As $\mathfrak{P}$ is an ideal, every $\mathcal{O}_K$-multiple of $p$ lies in $\mathfrak{P}$, hence $p\mathcal{O}_K\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$.

**Step 2: $\mathfrak{P}$ contains some factor $\mathfrak{P}_i$.**
Using the factorization $p\mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{P}_1\cdots\mathfrak{P}_n$, Step 1 gives
$$\mathfrak{P}_1\cdots\mathfrak{P}_n=p\mathcal{O}_K\subseteq\mathfrak{P}.$$
Thus the product $\mathfrak{P}_1\cdots\mathfrak{P}_n\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$. Since $\mathfrak{P}$ is a **prime** ideal, by definition: if an ideal product $IJ\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$ then $I\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$ or $J\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$. Iterating this across the $n$ factors, there exists some index $i$ with $\mathfrak{P}_i\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$.

**Step 3: $\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}_i$.**
The ring $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a Dedekind domain (ring of integers of a number field). In a Dedekind domain every nonzero prime ideal is **maximal**. Both $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}_i$ are nonzero prime ideals (they appear in the factorization of the nonzero ideal $p\mathcal{O}_K$, and $\mathfrak{P}$ lies above the rational prime $p$, hence is nonzero). The inclusion $\mathfrak{P}_i\subseteq\mathfrak{P}$ with $\mathfrak{P}_i$ maximal forces $\mathfrak{P}_i=\mathfrak{P}$.

**Conclusion.** Every prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$ lying above $p$ coincides with one of the factors $\mathfrak{P}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{P}_n$ in the prime decomposition of $p\mathcal{O}_K$. Equivalently, the factorization $p\mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{P}_1\cdots\mathfrak{P}_n$ exhausts all primes above $p$; there are no "extra" primes lying above $p$ beyond the factors appearing in the decomposition. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
